contraindications: Succinylcholine: hyperkalemia (potassium 5.6) with rhabdomyolysis; risk of hyperkalemic cardiac arrest; use a nondepolarizing agent.
Haloperidol, chlorpromazine and other antipsychotics: lower the seizure threshold, impair heat dissipation and cause neuroleptic malignant syndrome; avoid.
interactions: MDMA + buspirone: additive serotonergic effect; serotonin toxicity; stop buspirone.
Tramadol, meperidine, fentanyl, linezolid and methylene blue + MDMA: additional serotonergic load; avoid.
Cyproheptadine + benzodiazepines: additive sedation; cyproheptadine is anticholinergic and is given orally or by nasogastric tube only.
Levetiracetam + current medications: no clinically relevant interaction; maintenance dose by creatinine clearance (creatinine 2.2).
Fosphenytoin or phenytoin + current medications: no relevant pharmacokinetic interaction; less effective for drug-induced seizures.

output.query: Serotonin syndrome with seizures and hyperthermia; hyponatremia with seizures

results.finding: Serotonin toxicity is diagnosed by the Hunter criteria: in a patient exposed to a serotonergic agent, spontaneous clonus; inducible or ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; tremor with hyperreflexia; or hypertonia with a temperature above 38 C and ocular or inducible clonus.

Management is withdrawal of serotonergic drugs, benzodiazepines, active cooling and cyproheptadine (12 mg then 2 mg every 2 hours while symptoms continue); temperatures above 41.1 C call for sedation, nondepolarizing paralysis and intubation; antipyretics are not effective.
Hyponatremia with seizures is treated with 150 mL of 3% saline over 20 minutes, repeated up to twice, aiming for a 5 mmol/L rise in the first hour and no more than 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours.

output.summary: Serotonin toxicity is diagnosed with the Hunter criteria and treated by stopping serotonergic drugs, benzodiazepines, cooling and cyproheptadine, with paralysis and intubation above 41.1 C [Boyer_2005]. Hyponatremia with seizures is treated with 3% saline boluses, aiming for 5 mmol/L in the first hour and no more than 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours [Spasovski_2014].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sodium 124 with urine osmolality 480 and urine sodium 58; potassium 5.6 and creatinine 2.2; CK 8640 with dipstick blood and no RBC; lactate 11.4 with pH 7.13; urine amphetamines positive, other drugs negative
action_criteria.label: Emergency laboratory work-up: glucose, CBC, electrolytes, magnesium, renal and hepatic function, toxicology, CK
action_criteria.rationale: Glucose, electrolyte, renal and hepatic derangements are reversible causes of seizures and decide the ASM and its dose; toxicology identifies the drugs taken, and CK, potassium and serum and urine osmolality follow the rhabdomyolysis and the hyponatremia [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Mild diffuse cerebral edema with sulcal effacement, cisterns preserved; no hemorrhage
action_criteria.label: Non-contrast head CT after stabilization
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes hemorrhage, mass or edema that would change management, and must precede any LP [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Continuous generalized 2-4 Hz spike-and-wave with evolving frequency, time-locked to the convulsions
action_criteria.label: Continuous video-EEG to confirm ongoing seizures and monitor treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Convulsive SE with rigidity, and likely sedation or paralysis, needs EEG confirmation of seizure control, since convulsive SE may continue as non-convulsive SE; continuous monitoring for at least 24 hours [Brophy_2012]; terminology [ACNS_2021].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Diffuse mild cerebral swelling without restricted diffusion or focal lesion
action_criteria.label: MRI brain if encephalopathy persists after correction
action_criteria.rationale: The cause is established (MDMA with hyponatremia and serotonin toxicity); MRI is reserved for persistent encephalopathy after correction [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Buspirone is stopped as an added serotonergic drug; succinylcholine and antipsychotics are contraindicated; serotonergic analgesics and linezolid are avoided; levetiracetam is dosed for renal function
action_criteria.label: Drug-interaction check: MDMA and buspirone, cyproheptadine, intubation drugs and the second-line ASM
action_criteria.rationale: Buspirone adds to MDMA serotonin toxicity, and the drugs this patient may need (cyproheptadine, sedatives, a paralytic, analgesics) include ones that worsen it or the hyperkalemia [Boyer_2005].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on serotonin toxicity treatment and hypertonic saline for hyponatremia with seizures
action_criteria.label: Literature: serotonin syndrome and hyponatremia with seizures
action_criteria.rationale: Background evidence only; not a clinical step of the work-up.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not raise sodium by more than 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours [Spasovski_2014].
Do not give antipsychotics (haloperidol, chlorpromazine): they lower the seizure threshold and impair heat dissipation.
Do not use succinylcholine if intubation is needed: potassium 5.6 with rhabdomyolysis.
Do not rely on antipyretics for the hyperthermia; it is driven by muscle hyperactivity [Boyer_2005].
Do not give further serotonergic drugs (tramadol, meperidine, fentanyl, linezolid, methylene blue).
required_recommendations: Give a benzodiazepine now: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg per dose, repeat once), or IM midazolam 10 mg without IV access [Glauser_2016].

Give 150 mL of 3% saline over 20 minutes for hyponatremia with seizures, repeated up to twice while checking sodium, aiming for a rise of 5 mmol/L in the first hour and no more than 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours [Spasovski_2014].

Cool actively now (evaporative cooling, ice packs, cooled IV fluids) and control muscle activity with benzodiazepines; if temperature exceeds 41.1 C, sedate, paralyze with a nondepolarizing agent and intubate [Boyer_2005].
Stop buspirone and all serotonergic drugs and give cyproheptadine 12 mg by nasogastric tube, then 2 mg every 2 hours while symptoms continue [Boyer_2005].

Load a second-line ASM if seizures continue: IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (maximum 4500 mg), with maintenance by creatinine clearance; avoid fosphenytoin, which is less effective in drug-induced seizures [ESETT_2019].

Treat the rhabdomyolysis and AKI (CK 8640, creatinine 2.2) with IV isotonic fluids titrated to urine output while checking sodium every 2 to 4 hours, obtain an ECG and treat the potassium of 5.6, and involve nephrology if oliguria or hyperkalemia progresses.
Admit to an ICU and continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours after clinical and electrographic seizure control [Brophy_2012].

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
Polysomnography studies sleep disorders and has no role in the acute evaluation of status epilepticus.

accepted: MDMA-associated status epilepticus from severe hyponatremia (Na 124), hyperthermia, and serotonin syndrome

differential.key_features: Sodium 124 after heavy water intake explains seizures, but bilateral clonus, hypertonia, mydriasis, diaphoresis and 40.2 C on buspirone meet the Hunter criteria
Hours of dancing with 40.2 C and CK 8640 overlap with MDMA hyperthermia; it adds to, but does not replace, the toxic cause
Cocaine negative; the amphetamine immunoassay does not separate MDMA from methamphetamine, but the history names MDMA and the clonus points to a serotonergic agent
No antipsychotic exposure; clonus and hyperreflexia rather than bradyreflexic rigidity
Fever and leukocytosis are explained by the toxidrome and convulsions; no meningism; LP deferred because of the diffuse edema and reconsidered only if the course departs from the toxidrome

differential.diagnosis: First presentation of idiopathic generalized epilepsy
differential.key_features: No prior seizures; the toxic and metabolic causes explain the presentation

key_clinical_evidence: MDMA causes antidiuretic hormone release; with heavy water intake it produces acute hyponatremia (serum osmolality 270, urine osmolality 480, urine sodium 58)
Clonus, hypertonia, hyperthermia, mydriasis and diaphoresis after MDMA on buspirone meet the Hunter criteria for serotonin toxicity
Hyponatremia with seizures needs 3% saline boluses with the rise kept within 10 mmol/L in 24 hours
Isotonic fluids for rhabdomyolysis change the sodium and must be given with frequent sodium checks
Antipsychotics and succinylcholine are hazardous here; antipyretics do not work

labs.interpretation: Leukocytosis (WBC 16.8). Low sodium (124) with low serum osmolality (270); urine osmolality 480 and urine sodium 58. High potassium (5.6) and phosphate (5.2), low calcium (8.2). Raised BUN (26) and creatinine (2.2). Low bicarbonate (14) with raised anion gap (23) and very high lactate (11.4); metabolic acidemia on arterial gas (pH 7.13) with hypoxemia (pO2 56). Hyperglycemia (186). Markedly raised CK (8640) and uric acid (9.8). Raised AST (142) and ALT (88); INR 1.4. Urine dipstick blood 3+ with 0-2 RBC/hpf. Urine immunoassay positive for amphetamines; cocaine, opiates, cannabinoids, benzodiazepines and tricyclics negative; blood alcohol undetectable. Magnesium and albumin within reference ranges.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: 4 required actions (labs, CT, continuous EEG, drug check) with optional MRI and literature; MDMA-associated convulsive SE with acute hyponatremia, hyperthermia, serotonin toxicity on buspirone and rhabdomyolysis with AKI; teaching points are hypertonic saline within the correction limit, cooling and cyproheptadine, fluids that interact with the sodium, and drugs to avoid (antipsychotics, succinylcholine, serotonergic agents); 2 grounded red herrings.

patient.chief_complaint: Campus police and EMS called after student found convulsing in dormitory hallway, 12 minutes duration

social_history.drugs: Reports recreational MDMA use at party last night

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. White is a 24-year-old college student with no prior epilepsy who is brought by campus EMS after being found convulsing in his dormitory hallway by a friend. The friend reports that the patient attended an off-campus party last night where he used MDMA (3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine, ecstasy) approximately 8 hours prior to seizure onset. The friend says he danced for hours and drank large amounts of water through the night. He appears to have developed a seizure while returning to his room. The friend estimated continuous seizure activity for approximately 12 minutes before EMS arrived. No prior seizures. He is on buspirone for anxiety. His temperature on arrival is 40.2°C.
